passage:
Monday: Joseph's hands shook as he played scales for his music teacher, Parveen. "My recital's on Saturday," he whispered. "I'm going to mess up."
Wednesday: Parveen taught him a routine: three slow breaths, shake out his hands, and look at one friendly face. He practised it before each piece.
Saturday: Backstage, his stomach fluttered. He breathed slowly three times, shook his hands and found his mother in the crowd. He played, missed one note, and kept going. Afterwards he said, "I was still nervous, but it didn't stop me."

qa.q: When was Joseph's recital?
qa.a: His recital was on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Joseph saying "I'm going to mess up" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he was anxious and expected to fail.

qa.q: What routine helped Joseph?
qa.a: Three slow breaths, shaking out his hands and looking at one friendly face.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel after the recital?
qa.a: Parveen would likely feel proud that Joseph used the routine and kept going after a mistake. 🎉

grounding: It shows a child recognising nervousness before a recital and using a calming routine over time.

passage: "Zubin, I was so nervous before my board exams that I couldn't eat breakfast. My hands were cold, my mind went blank when I saw the paper. So I made myself a routine. I'd sip water, close my eyes, and breathe slowly, counting. Then I'd read each question twice before writing a word. And I'd start with the easiest question, to warm up. It didn't make the nerves disappear, but they got smaller. Now you try it before your test tomorrow." Varun Chacha squeezed his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Varun do before writing an answer?
qa.a: He read each question twice.

qa.q: What does Varun mean when he says the nerves got smaller?
qa.a: He means he still felt anxious, but the routine helped him feel calmer and more in control.

qa.q: What advice does Varun give Zubin?
qa.a: He suggests sipping water, breathing slowly, reading questions twice and starting with the easiest one.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing that his uncle was nervous too?
qa.a: He might feel less alone and more hopeful about handling his own nerves.

grounding: An elder tells a story of exam nervousness and a calming routine.

passage: The school bus was stuck in traffic on the morning of the maths exam. Ramesh's knee bounced. "We'll be late. I'll forget everything." Shankar, his friend, looked at him. "Remember what Miss said? Slow breath in, slow breath out." Ramesh tried. Once. Twice. His knee slowed. "Now tell me one formula," Shankar said. Ramesh recited the area of a rectangle. By the time they reached school, just in time, he felt steadier. He walked into the exam hall still nervous but calmer.

qa.q: What was stuck in traffic?
qa.a: The school bus was stuck in traffic.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's bouncing knee suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was anxious about being late and forgetting everything.

qa.q: How did Shankar help Ramesh calm down?
qa.a: Shankar reminded him to breathe slowly and asked him to recite a formula.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel helping Ramesh?
qa.a: Shankar may feel glad to be a good friend and a bit calmer himself.

grounding: It shows a child recognising exam nerves and using calming breaths under time pressure.

passage: The colony hall smelled of jasmine and dust. Devika, ten, stood behind the curtain in her dance costume, and her tummy was doing flips. 'My hands are cold,' she whispered. She knew this feeling now. It came before tests too. Manjula maasi had taught her a trick. Devika pressed both feet into the floor, felt the cool tiles and breathed in while counting to four, then out to four. Once, twice, five times. She hummed the first line of the song under her breath. Through the gap in the curtain she saw Maasi in the second row, holding up a thumb. Her heart was still quick, but her hands had stopped shaking when the music began.

qa.q: What did Devika hum under her breath?
qa.a: She hummed the first line of the song.

qa.q: How can you tell Devika recognised her nervousness?
qa.a: She noticed her cold hands and flipping tummy and thought she knew this feeling from before tests.

qa.q: What in Devika's routine could help other children before a performance?
qa.a: Pressing feet into the floor, slow counted breaths and rehearsing the first line are simple steps anyone can use.

qa.q: What might Manjula maasi have felt watching from the second row?
qa.a: She was likely a little nervous for Devika too, and proud to see her use the trick she had taught.

grounding: Shows a child recognising nervousness before a recital and using a calming routine.

passage: 'Bhaiya, I can't sleep.' 'Spelling test?' Varun nodded. 'My hands are all sweaty. What if I forget everything?' Nitin, sixteen, shut his laptop. 'Okay. Where do you feel it?' 'Here.' Varun touched his chest. 'Like a drum.' 'That's your body getting ready. Happens to me before board practicals.' 'Really?' 'Really. Let's do the balloon thing. Breathe into your tummy, slowly. Now let it out like a tyre going flat.' Varun giggled but did it. 'Again.' Three more. 'Now tell me three words you know for sure.' 'Because. Friend. Beautiful.' 'See? They're in there.' Varun lay back. 'The drum is smaller now.' 'Good. Tomorrow, same balloon before you start.'

qa.q: Which three words did Varun say he knew for sure?
qa.a: He said 'because', 'friend' and 'beautiful'.

qa.q: What was Varun worried about before the test?
qa.a: He was afraid he would forget all his spellings, and he felt it as sweaty hands and a drumming chest.

qa.q: Which parts of Nitin's help could Varun reuse on his own?
qa.a: He can notice where he feels the nerves, do slow balloon breaths and remind himself of words he knows.

qa.q: What might change if Nitin had just said 'Stop worrying and sleep'?
qa.a: Varun would likely have felt brushed off, with no way to calm the drum, and might have lain awake longer.

grounding: Shows a child naming exam nervousness and learning a calming breathing routine with a sibling's help.
